paras: The attempted lynching of Willis S. Delaire took place near Polk City, Iowa, in late June 1882, when a masked band of twelve men seized Delaire, a young man held on suspicion in the murder of the town's mayor, and hanged him from a tree five times until he confessed. Delaire survived, said the confession was invented to save his life, was acquitted, and sued the men who hanged him. The case drew national notice first as a solved murder and then as a civil suit against lynchers.

R. W. Stubbs, mayor of Polk City, was shot dead in his house at about three in the morning on a Saturday in April 1882 by two intruders who were evidently after money he kept there. A Chicago Times special reported that the town had a "well organized company of vigilantees" out in force, and a Des Moines dispatch denied rumors that the murderers had been lynched.

According to a Des Moines dispatch of June 27, Delaire was arrested at the depot in Polk City the previous night on suspicion of the murder. In his own account, given later to a Des Moines Register reporter at the city jail, he said a Mr. Terrell, who was not a peace officer, arrested him and kept him at his house, and in the evening enlisted a Polk City man to help guard him. About nine o'clock, as the party walked down the road, a masked man appeared, followed by eleven others.

The band put a sack over Delaire's head and dragged him about a quarter of a mile along a wagon road to a grove, where they threw a rope over a low limb and hauled him up until he fell insensible. Questioned about the Stubbs murder, he denied it four times, and on the fifth hanging he told a story that a gang of fifteen had plotted the robbery and that a Missourian named Wyckes or Wickes had fired the shot. The Register account said the men wanted "to only scare" him, but that another attempt would likely have killed him.

Delaire told the Register that he and the others he had named were in Chariton on the night of the murder, and that he knew the men who had hanged him and had proof of who they were. By late July he had been set free, released on a writ of habeas corpus, and an August dispatch said he was acquitted of the charges based on his confession. He then brought suit against members of the band, for $25,000 according to the Des Moines wire, for $40,000 according to the Oskaloosa Herald, while the Billings Herald counted three suits for false imprisonment and the hanging.

No report of an arrest or criminal charge against the men who hanged him, or of the outcome of his suits, appears in the coverage. In December 1882 John Weir of Prairie City was arrested and said he had driven William Kline and a man named Wilcox to Polk City to rob Stubbs, and that Kline admitted the killing.

Only white newspapers covered the case, and none of them stated Delaire's race. The June wire, which the Savannah Morning News headed "A MYSTERY CLEARED UP," treated the confession as the solution of the murder and mentioned the threat of lynching only as the way it was obtained. The Register's jail interview mocked the night as a "lynching matinee" with Delaire as its "principal" while setting out his claim of innocence, and it was reprinted in July under the heading "HANGED FIVE TIMES."

The August 8 Des Moines wire, which called the attackers "a mob of Polk county merchants," ran from Washington to Memphis and Dakota under headlines such as "Civil Suit Against Lynchers" and "Prosecuting His Persecutors." A news summary headed "CONFESSING A MURDER OF WHICH HE WAS NOT GUILTY" said the torture had compelled his confession, and Baltimore's German-language Deutsche Correspondent called him completely innocent and hoped he would win his damages.
The June dispatch reported Delaire's confession as fact, but his later account, his release and his acquittal treated it as false, and the December arrests named other men.

bases: A masked band of twelve seized Delaire from a private guard and hanged him from a tree limb five times to force a confession, an attempted lynching in the papers' own words (A17, A18, A24).
A band of twelve with no legal authority hanged Delaire repeatedly over the Stubbs murder, but he survived, so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one (A17, A18, A24).

The June 27 Des Moines wire (confession 'under threat of lynching'), Delaire's Register interview, and the August 8 wire (drawn up to a tree by the neck by a mob) agree on the seizure and the coerced confession (A3, A18, A24).
